options.text: The reactant that is present in the largest amount
The reactant that is completely used up first, determining the amount of product formed
The reactant that is the most expensive
The reactant that reacts the slowest

questions.explanation: The limiting reactant is the one that is completely used up first in a reaction. It limits the amount of product that can be formed, regardless of how much of the other reactant(s) is present.

options.text: The reactant that runs out first
The reactant that is left over after the reaction is complete
The product of the reaction
The catalyst

questions.explanation: The excess reactant is the one that is not completely used up during the reaction. Some of it remains after the limiting reactant has been consumed.

questions.stem: In the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, if you have 1 mole of Mg and 1 mole of HCl, which is the limiting reactant?

options.text: Magnesium (Mg)
Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
Both are limiting
Neither is limiting

questions.explanation: The equation shows 1 mole of Mg needs 2 moles of HCl. With only 1 mole of HCl available but 2 needed, HCl will run out first and is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: How do you determine which reactant is limiting?

options.text: The one with the smallest mass is always limiting
Calculate the moles of each reactant and compare with the mole ratio from the balanced equation
The one listed first in the equation is always limiting
The one with the highest Mr is always limiting

questions.explanation: To find the limiting reactant, calculate the moles of each reactant and compare them to the ratio required by the balanced equation. The one that runs out first is limiting.

questions.stem: When a reaction stops because the limiting reactant has been used up, what can you conclude?

options.text: All reactants have been completely consumed
The excess reactant remains unreacted
No products have been formed
The reaction has reached equilibrium

questions.explanation: When the limiting reactant is used up, the reaction stops. The excess reactant(s) will remain unreacted because there is nothing left for them to react with.

questions.stem: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, if 3 moles of H₂ react with 1 mole of O₂, which is limiting?

options.text: Hydrogen (H₂)
Oxygen (O₂)
Both are limiting equally
Water is limiting

questions.explanation: The equation needs 2 moles of H₂ for every 1 mole of O₂. With 3 moles of H₂, you would need 1.5 moles of O₂, but only 1 mole is available. Oxygen runs out first, so it is limiting.

questions.stem: Why is it important to identify the limiting reactant in industrial chemistry?

options.text: To make the reaction go faster
To determine the maximum amount of product that can be made and reduce waste
To change the products of the reaction
To increase the temperature of the reaction

questions.explanation: Identifying the limiting reactant tells you the maximum amount of product possible. In industry, this helps optimise the use of expensive reactants and minimise waste.
